title: Looking Up at the Clouds
cardDescription: Look upward through a crossword about familiar sky colors, cloud shapes, and the words used to describe visibility.
description: Look upward through a crossword about familiar sky colors, cloud shapes, and the words used to describe visibility.
focus: The clues name visible forms in the sky and describe how light reaches the ground. A cloud name appears alongside sky colors and everyday visibility words.
solvingTip: Ask whether the clue describes a cloud type, a shape, a color, or a condition. Short sky words can give useful crossings for the longer cloud names.
words: Visible mass of tiny water droplets or ice crystals in the air
Cloud type commonly pictured as a puffy heap
High thin wispy cloud made mainly of ice crystals
Cloud type forming a broad low layer
Cloudlike droplets near the ground that reduce visibility
Suspended tiny droplets producing lighter obscuration than fog
Reduced clarity caused by fine particles in the air
The visible expanse above the ground
Color often seen overhead on a clear day
Color commonly used to describe a dull overcast sky
Color of many sunlit puffy clouds
Describing a sky with little or no cloud cover
Describing a sky covered by clouds
Small rounded mass resembling a cumulus cloud
Star whose light reaches Earth during the day
Visible illumination coming from the sky

answerNotes.CUMULUS: Cumulus clouds often have a heaped or puffy appearance. The clue uses that recognizable shape.
answerNotes.CIRRUS: Cirrus clouds are high and wispy, usually composed of ice crystals. Their thin streaks differ from a broad low cloud layer.
answerNotes.STRATUS: Stratus describes a layered cloud form. A low broad sheet gives the shape and position used in the clue.
answerNotes.FOG: Fog consists of suspended droplets near the surface. Its position and effect on visibility distinguish it from a cloud seen high above.
answerNotes.HAZE: Haze can result from fine particles rather than water droplets alone. That difference separates it from the fog definition.
answerNotes.OVERCAST: Overcast describes extensive cloud cover. It is a condition of the sky rather than the name of one cloud.

title: Rain at the Window
cardDescription: Listen to a rainy day through familiar words for falling water, wet surfaces, and the objects around a home.
description: Listen to a rainy day through familiar words for falling water, wet surfaces, and the objects around a home.
focus: This puzzle combines rainfall descriptions with the places water collects or runs. Some answers name an object, while others name a sound, a movement, or a degree of wetness.
solvingTip: Check whether the clue asks for falling water, a place it gathers, a sound, or an object. Short wet-weather words can help cross longer rain descriptions.
words: One small rounded amount of falling rain
Very light rain made of fine droplets
Small shallow pool of rainwater on the ground
To scatter water by striking or stepping into it
Small wave spreading across a puddle
Covered with or containing liquid water
Slightly wet rather than fully soaked
Handheld canopy used to keep off rain
Outer garment designed to shed falling water
Channel along a roof edge that carries away rainwater
Opening or pipe through which water flows away
Upper covering of a house receiving the rain
Glass opening against which rain may patter
Long narrow mark left by running water on glass
To fall in small separate drops
Soft repeated tapping sound of light rain

answerNotes.DRIZZLE: Drizzle consists of fine falling droplets. Downpour describes heavy rain, so the intensity words distinguish them.
answerNotes.SHOWER: Shower means a period of rainfall here. It is not the indoor washing fixture with the same name.
answerNotes.PUDDLE: A puddle is a shallow collection of water. It names the result on the ground rather than the rain falling into it.
answerNotes.GUTTER: A roof gutter channels runoff. Its position at the roof edge distinguishes it from the drain that carries water away.
answerNotes.DAMP: Damp means slightly wet. Soaked describes a much greater amount of moisture.
answerNotes.PATTER: Patter names a repeated light tapping sound. The clue asks for what is heard rather than the visible drops.

title: A Breeze Through the Trees
cardDescription: Follow a breeze through familiar words for wind strength, direction, and the things moving around it.
description: Follow a breeze through familiar words for wind strength, direction, and the things moving around it.
focus: The clues connect moving air with visible signs such as fluttering fabric and bending branches. Some answers describe wind itself; others describe an action, a marker, or a direction.
solvingTip: Look for whether the clue asks for strength, direction, an object, or a movement. A steady light wind and a sudden stronger burst have different names.
words: Sudden brief increase in wind strength
Condition with little or no wind
Current of air felt through an opening indoors
Turning device showing the direction from which wind blows
Fabric marker that flutters from a pole in the wind
Light framed object flown on a line in moving air
Flat plant part that may flutter in a breeze
To move gently back and forth in the wind
To curve under the force of a strong gust
To move loosely back and forth, as a flag
To make a soft dry sound, as windblown leaves
High clear sound wind may make through a narrow gap
How fast the wind is moving
The way from which the wind comes
Compass direction in which the sun generally sets

answerNotes.GUST: A gust is a short stronger burst within the wind. Breeze describes a gentler overall flow.
answerNotes.VANE: A weather vane shows wind direction. It differs from an anemometer, which measures wind speed.
answerNotes.DRAFT: Draft is a current of air here. It is not a preliminary written version or a selection process.
answerNotes.CALM: Calm describes little or no wind in this setting. The clue uses a weather condition rather than a person's mood.
answerNotes.DIRECTION: Wind direction is conventionally named for where the air comes from. A north wind comes from the north.
answerNotes.GALE: Gale describes very strong wind. The clue uses the ordinary word without asking for a numerical wind-scale range.

title: Snow on a Winter Morning
cardDescription: Picture a snowy morning through familiar frozen-water forms, winter objects, and the words for freezing and melting.
description: Picture a snowy morning through familiar frozen-water forms, winter objects, and the words for freezing and melting.
focus: The clues distinguish falling precipitation from ice on a surface or water on the ground. American weather usage determines the meaning of terms such as sleet.
solvingTip: Check whether a clue names something falling, something formed on a surface, or an action. Short cold-weather and clothing words can help cross longer ice forms.
words: Frozen precipitation falling as ice crystals or flakes
One small piece of falling snow
Ice crystals forming on a cold surface
U.S. weather term for falling ice pellets
Ice balls growing in storm clouds and falling to the ground
To change water from liquid to solid
To become unfrozen as temperature rises
Partly melted snow mixed with water
Hanging taper of ice formed by freezing dripping water
Heap of snow piled by the wind
Color commonly associated with freshly fallen snow
Winter hand covering with a shared space for the fingers
Long cloth wrapped around the neck on a wintry day
Footwear rising above the ankle for a winter outing
Outer garment put on before going into cold weather
Runner-supported vehicle that slides over snow
Broad-bladed tool used to move snow

answerNotes.SLEET: In U.S. forecasting, sleet means ice pellets. British usage can instead refer to a mixture of rain and snow.
answerNotes.HAIL: Hailstones grow in storm clouds. They differ from sleet pellets formed when falling water freezes before reaching the ground.
answerNotes.FROST: Frost forms as ice crystals on a surface. Snow falls from clouds, so the location of formation distinguishes the clues.
answerNotes.THAW: Thaw means become unfrozen. It is the opposite change from freezing.
answerNotes.SLUSH: Slush is a wet mixture of partly melted snow and water. It differs from solid clear ice.
answerNotes.DRIFT: A snowdrift is a wind-built heap. Drift can also describe slow movement, but the clue asks for the accumulated snow.

title: Reading the Weather Report
cardDescription: Explore a weather report through familiar map terms, pressure labels, and words for expected conditions.
description: Explore a weather report through familiar map terms, pressure labels, and words for expected conditions.
focus: This puzzle defines forecast vocabulary rather than presenting a live forecast. Clues describe map features, atmospheric conditions, measuring systems, and ways of reporting expectations.
solvingTip: Ask whether the clue names a map feature, a condition, a report term, or a likelihood word. Short map words can help cross longer forecast terms.
words: System that uses radio waves to help locate precipitation
Drawing showing the area covered by a weather report
Mark used on a map to represent a weather condition
Boundary between air masses with different characteristics
Atmospheric force measured by a barometer
Unit used to state a temperature
Weather-map label for a region of greater atmospheric pressure
Weather-map label for a region of lower atmospheric pressure
Amount of water vapor in the air
Likelihood that an event will occur
General view of expected future conditions
Account describing observed or expected weather
New information added to an earlier forecast
Relating to the nearby area rather than a distant region

answerNotes.BAROMETER: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure. A thermometer measures temperature, so the measured quantity distinguishes them.
answerNotes.FRONT: A weather front is a boundary between air masses. It is not the front side of a building in this map context.
answerNotes.RADAR: Weather radar helps locate precipitation using radio-wave signals. It is a measuring system rather than a cloud type.
answerNotes.PERCENT: Percent means per hundred. A percentage expresses a proportion rather than a temperature unit.
answerNotes.CHANCE: Chance describes likelihood. It is not a promise that a weather event will or will not happen.
answerNotes.HUMIDITY: Humidity concerns water vapor. Relative humidity is commonly reported as a percentage, but the general word does not itself specify that one measure.
